Volume 17 · Chapter 09

Research supervision and mentoring

Professional Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v17-c08

By the endGuide research toward independence with explicit responsibilities and ethical boundaries.

Volume 17 · Chapter 9

Research supervision and mentoring

Capability. Negotiate a feasible research scope, give feedback that improves an economic argument, document contributions and disagreements, and assess growing independence without taking over the learner's research.

Prerequisites. The diagnostic, feedback and learning-evidence distinctions of Chapter 8, the assessment design of Chapter 5, and the research-contract discipline of Volume 16, Chapter 1. Weighted means and a concave quadratic are derived below. Both cases, all exchanges and all learner responses are original synthetic specimens. No actual supervision, learner improvement or ethical approval is claimed.

1. Supervision is a relationship with inspectable work

A supervisor may know the answer to a student's immediate problem. Supplying that answer is not the same as enabling the student to formulate and defend the next argument. Supervision combines responsibility for the quality and boundaries of a project with the development of the researcher's judgment. Mentoring can also include advice about professional direction and participation. A mentor need not be the formal supervisor or assessor; identify which role a person is performing and what decisions they can actually make.

The Office of Research Integrity's introduction to mentor and trainee responsibilities describes mutual responsibilities, supportive conditions, supervision and preparation for independent research. It also recognizes potential disputes about time, credit and results. We use this as bounded professional guidance, not as a tested causal claim that a particular meeting schedule produces better researchers.

A scope agreement specifies the question, target quantity or proposition, available inputs, proposed method, deliverable and exclusions. A milestone is an inspectable intermediate product with a review criterion and an owner, not merely a date. A decision log records a substantive choice, its reason, alternatives, evidence and who made it. A contribution ledger records actual intellectual and practical contributions as they occur; it is evidence for a credit discussion, not an automatic authorship calculator. An independence check asks the learner to explain or extend an argument under stated support conditions.

Write the question at the scale of the available evidence. “Measure the contribution of changing group weights to an observed average” can be completed with a small supplied table. “Identify the causal effect of a training program on wages” requires a design and data that the table does not supply. A narrow correct result is a legitimate milestone; broadening the title does not create identification. Similarly, proving a global optimum in a small model may be valuable training without demonstrating that the model describes an industry.

The agreement should separate the student's project from paid assistance on the supervisor's other projects. Record expected work, feedback turnaround, meeting preparation, access, tools, data handling and how changes will be negotiated. The ORI basic-responsibilities guidance recommends early clarity about expectations, performance criteria, shared duties, data procedures and credit. It explicitly recognizes unequal power and places responsibility on mentors to raise sensitive questions. Our schedules below are proposed local arrangements, not employment rules, institutional deadlines or universal authorship standards.

2. Give feedback on an argument, then return responsibility

Read the student's actual work before prescribing more reading. Locate the claim, the evidence or proof step offered for it, and the smallest missing warrant. Distinguish a clerical error from a wrong target or an invalid implication. Explain why the issue matters, demonstrate only the amount needed to make the repair accessible, and ask for a revision that makes the corrected reasoning visible. “Be more rigorous” names no action; “compare the best positive-output payoff with zero, because the derivative omits the fixed participation cost” does.

Use a meeting to reach a decision, not to produce a transcript of everything the supervisor knows. A proposed 30-minute structure is: five minutes for the student's question and previous decision; ten for one argument; ten for competing repairs; five to assign the next product and record unresolved issues. If the project requires more extensive review, renegotiate the allocation rather than silently expanding student labor. Written feedback can precede the meeting, and the student can submit a written defense when spontaneous speech would obscure the reasoning being assessed.

After a worked repair, reduce help on the next task. First the learner explains the correction, then applies the method to a changed input, then chooses between methods for a new question. Record prompts, code assistance, coauthor input and supplied calculations. A correct copied proof demonstrates access to a proof; an independently explained extension is different evidence. Neither a single transfer response nor fluency licenses a general declaration of research independence. Use several dated artifacts, including recognition of a limit or an error.

Separate project quality from the learner's progress. A supervisor may need to repair a consequential public calculation immediately, while documenting that the repair was theirs. The student's subsequent revision and new task can still reveal learning. Do not withhold a known material error from a public report to create an assessment opportunity. Conversely, polishing the whole student's draft and then calling it independently produced erases the evidence the supervision was supposed to develop.

3. Credit, authority and disagreement

Intellectual criticism should address the argument and its assumptions. The AEA Code of Professional Conduct, adopted April 20, 2018, emphasizes honest and transparent research, limits of expertise, conflicts of interest, respectful discussion and fair treatment. It supports this professional stance; it does not establish this chapter's authorship order, a particular institution's complaint procedure or legal rights over data.

Discuss credit before work begins and revisit it when contributions change. In these cases, routine supervision alone is not treated as an automatic promise of coauthorship, and providing access alone does not settle author status. These are proposed agreements that must be checked against the actual discipline, venue and institution. Record who originated the question, developed an identification argument or proof, built data, wrote code and drafted or substantively revised text. Discuss responsibility for the submitted argument as well as recognition. Authorship, acknowledgement, data access, intellectual property and employment obligations are distinct questions; one label does not resolve the others.

A conflict protocol should give a concrete next step and an alternative when approaching the supervisor is unsafe or inappropriate. Preserve relevant versions and factual records through authorized channels; do not circulate private complaints or restricted data broadly. Seek clarification of the disputed task or credit decision, propose an interim arrangement that protects necessary access and deadlines, and identify an appropriate independent program or institutional contact. Verify that contact's role and confidentiality limits before sharing sensitive material. The chapter cannot promise confidentiality, anonymity, non-retaliation outcomes or a particular remedy.

A supervisor who is the subject of a complaint should not make the learner's access to advice conditional on first resolving it privately. Allegations of harassment, coercion, serious integrity problems or urgent safety concerns may require a different route from an ordinary scheduling dispute. Use the actual institution's available reporting and support processes; obtain appropriate specialist advice where needed. Do not infer misconduct from a mathematical error or a disagreement over a model. The cases below propose an ordinary work-dispute protocol while explicitly preserving those alternative routes.

4. Two complete supervision records

Case A — an aggregate wage increase is not a program effect

Initial agreement, proposed for a four-week exercise. Student Mira owns the analysis and first draft; supervisor Arun reviews the target and reasoning. The question is: “How much of the change in this synthetic workforce's mean hourly wage is attributable arithmetically to within-group wage changes and changing group shares?” Deliver a two-page descriptive memo, the exact calculation table, a reproducible calculation and a limitation statement. Exclude causal program evaluation, individual wage trajectories and welfare conclusions. The data below are invented public teaching inputs in currency units per hour; no personal records or access application is needed. Outside real data require a new access and scope review before use.

Allocate six student hours each week, including a 30-minute meeting. Mira sends the current artifact and two questions one working day before that meeting; Arun returns prioritized comments within two working days after it. If either cannot meet a date, notify the other and revise the plan explicitly. This is a proposed mutual schedule, not evidence of actual availability. Keep the original table, a versioned calculation and a short decision log. Calculators and code are permitted; disclose substantive help. Mira must explain every transformation and solve the independent task below without receiving its solution.

Synthetic hourly wages and workforce shares
GroupInitial wageFinal wageInitial shareFinal share
L20224/51/5
H40441/54/5

Primitive input, ordered initial wages, final wages, initial L share and final L share: (20,40,22,44,4/5,1/5). The second group's share is one minus the first. The groups have consistent definitions, wages are measured on the same nominal basis, and these are exact synthetic summaries. They contain no sampling model, price index, assignment mechanism or linked-person records.

Four inspectable milestones within six hours per week
WeekStudent product and pass criterionSupervisor action
1Question contract and weighted-mean table; units and each denominator correctCheck descriptive scope and table, identify one target error
2Exact decomposition and proof of identity; components sum to observed changeChallenge the choice of reference weights and causal language
3Revised two-page memo and contribution log; every claim matched to evidenceReturn one substantive review, preserving student wording where sound
4Independent changed-data task and oral or written defense; explain what is and is not learnedRecord reasoning and help used; agree next scope or remediation

Student draft. “Average wages rose from24 to39.6. Growth is65%, so the training program caused a65% improvement in worker pay. Both groups increased by10%, confirming the program effect. Changing group shares is a nuisance and can be ignored.”

Full supervisor feedback. “Your two aggregate means and growth rate are correct. Your target changes in the next sentence: an observed change in workforce composition is included in the aggregate, whereas ‘improvement in worker pay’ suggests a fixed set of people, and ‘caused’ requires a counterfactual design. Neither is supplied. Keep the correct aggregate calculation. Recompute the final mean using initial shares, derive the additive decomposition below and replace the causal sentence with a descriptive statement. Explain why even the fixed-share10% is not a program effect. Bring one alternative reference-weight decomposition and identify what remains unchanged. I have supplied the decomposition method; record that assistance, then produce and defend the revision yourself.”

Complete economic repair. Write wgt for group g's mean wage and sgt for its share, with shares nonnegative and summing to1 in each period. The observed mean is μt=Σgsgtwgt. Here μ0=24 and μ1=198/5, so the change is78/5 and proportional growth is(78/5)/24=13/20. The fixed-initial-share final mean is μ1|0=Σsg0wg1=132/5, giving growth1/10. Results are (24,198/5,132/5,13/20,1/10).

Add and subtract Σsg0wg1 in μ1−μ0. The exact identity is Σsg0(wg1−wg0)+Σ(sg1−sg0)wg1. The first term is(4/5)2+(1/5)4=12/5; the second is(−3/5)22+(3/5)44=66/5. Their sum is78/5. These are currency-per-hour contributions, not percentage points until divided by μ0. Dividing gives10 and55 percentage points of the65% aggregate growth. The component tuple is (12/5,66/5,78/5).

Using final shares for the wage term instead yields Σsg1Δwg=18/5 and initial wages for the share term yields ΣΔsgwg0=12. Thus (18/5,12,78/5) has the same total but different component allocation. The interaction ΣΔsΔw=6/5 moves between the two components. There is no unique causal attribution hidden in a choice of accounting order. Constant shares make the composition component zero; identical group wage changes can still coexist with a composition effect if wage levels differ. Percentage growth requires a nonzero baseline; a positive-wage interpretation here uses μ0>0.

Student's full revised claim. “In the supplied synthetic summaries the mean hourly wage rises from24 to39.6, a65% descriptive increase. At initial group shares the final mean would be26.4, a10% increase. With initial-share weighting for wage changes, within-group changes contribute2.4 currency units per hour and share changes contribute13.2; their sum is15.6. Alternative reference weights allocate the interaction differently. The table does not track the same individuals, supply a counterfactual for a program, or adjust nominal wages for prices. Neither65% nor10% identifies a causal program effect.”

Independent task and full benchmark. Hold shares fixed at the table's two period-specific vectors but replace final wages by21 and38: (20,40,21,38,4/5,1/5). Ask Mira to select the appropriate quantities for the same descriptive question and explain a falling group wage alongside a rising aggregate. The final mean is173/5, fixed-share final mean122/5, aggregate growth53/120 and fixed-share growth1/60. The initial-weight wage contribution is2/5 and final-wage share contribution51/5, total53/5. Thus (173/5,122/5,53/120,1/60,2/5,51/5,53/5). H's wage falls from40 to38 while its share rises; the aggregate can rise because it remains the higher-wage group. This establishes a calculation and interpretation benchmark, not an observed student's success.

Contribution and conflict record. Mira formulated the descriptive question and wrote the initial calculation; Arun supplied the decomposition teaching step and identified the causal overclaim. The revised memo must acknowledge the assistance in its learning log. For this teaching exercise Mira remains responsible for the submitted work; there is no journal authorship decision. If later joint research develops, discuss actual contributions, venue criteria and accountability before submission rather than converting supervisory rank into automatic authorship. If Arun instead requests an unplanned20-hour cleaning task for another project, Mira's proposed reply is: “Our current agreement allocates six hours weekly to this descriptive memo. Please separate the new project, its duties, credit and applicable arrangements. I propose retaining the current milestones until a revised agreement is made.” If unresolved, seek a program adviser or other verified independent contact; preserve the agreement and changes, and avoid putting sensitive data in the dispute record.

Case B — the derivative finds scale, not entry

Scope agreement. Student Leon will prove the global production choice in a one-period price-taking toy model, including capacity and an avoidable fixed operating cost. Supervisor Sal will review one proof draft and one revision over three weeks, with four student hours per week including a30-minute meeting. Deliver a two-page proposition/proof, a parameter table, a counterexample to an incorrect claim and a changed-parameter defense. Exclude estimation, strategic interaction and claims of a new publishable theorem. All quantities are invented; q is output units per period, a is net revenue per unit before the quadratic cost, b has units making bq²/2 a currency payoff, K is capacity and F is currency per period.

Assume a≥0, b>0, K>0 and F≥0. If the firm chooses q=0, its payoff is0 and it avoids F. If0<q≤K, payoff is J(q)=aq−bq²/2−F. The outside option must remain available. F is not a sunk cost in this model. The primary input is (6,2,4,5), ordered(a,b,K,F).

Milestones and support limits. Week1: Leon states the domain, differentiates the positive-output branch and submits a candidate table; Sal tests the outside option. Week2: Leon supplies a global proof with all boundary and tie cases; Sal identifies any unsupported implication and marks where the supervisor supplied an argument. Week3: Leon completes the new parameter task without a supplied solution, explains a failed conjecture and proposes a limited next question. Sal evaluates the reasoning and agrees further work or a repair. A missed meeting triggers a written update and revised date, not automatic expansion of the weekly allocation. Preserve versions, hand checks and any code used; code can check cases but cannot substitute for the global proof.

Student proof draft. “J′(q)=a−bq and J″(q)=−b<0. Therefore q=a/b is the unique global optimum for every fixed cost F. With a=6 and b=2, the firm chooses3 units. Capacity does not matter because the function is concave.”

Full supervisor feedback. “The derivatives are correct on the positive-output branch. Strict concavity there identifies the best operating scale only when it is feasible. It does not compare operating with avoiding F at q=0. Your formula also exceeds capacity when a/b>K. First maximize gross operating surplus G(q)=aq−bq²/2 over the feasible interval. Then compare its best value minus F with zero. State the ties explicitly. Do not appeal to a global differentiable J across0: with F>0 the operating branch has a downward jump immediately to the right of0. I am supplying this two-stage strategy, not a completed independent proof. Revise the proposition yourself, give a fixed-cost counterexample and then solve the unseen task.”

Complete revised proposition and proof. For a>0, put q*=min{K,a/b}, which is strictly positive. Completing the square gives G(q)=a²/(2b)−(b/2)(q−a/b)². If a/b≤K, the unique gross maximizer is a/b. If a/b>K, the squared distance decreases as q approaches K from below, so K uniquely maximizes gross surplus. This proves the candidate globally without relying only on a first-order condition. Its gross value S is a²/(2b) in the unconstrained branch and aK−bK²/2 in the capacity branch.

Every positive feasible q satisfies J(q)≤S−F, with equality only at q*. Hence if S>F, q* uniquely beats the outside option; if S<F, zero uniquely beats every positive q; if S=F, exactly0 and q* maximize payoff. There is no interval of tie quantities because G is strictly concave with a unique maximizer. When a=0, every positive q has J(q)=−bq²/2−F<0, including F=0, so q=0 uniquely wins. This handles the case in which a “best positive scale” at zero would not be feasible on the positive branch. Equality a/b=K belongs to either gross-value formula and both agree. K=0 and b≤0 are outside the stated model, not silently covered cases.

At the supplied input q*=3, S=9 and J(3)=4, so operate at3. Raising only F to9 gives a tie between0 and3; raising it to10 gives unique nonentry. Reducing only K to2 while keeping F=5 gives q*=2, S=8 and net3. These gross/net pairs are (3,9,4,3,9,0,3,9,-1,2,8,3); the third candidate's negative net makes0 the actual choice. Fixed cost changes entry, not the best operating scale conditional on operation. Capacity changes both feasible scale and attainable surplus.

Comparative-static extension and its limit. For a>0, increasing a weakly raises the best scale min{K,a/b} and strictly raises gross surplus S: for a₂>a₁>0, using the old positive optimum gives G(q*₁;a₂)=S(a₁)+(a₂−a₁)q*₁>S(a₁). Thus the set of a supporting operation expands as profitability rises, holding other primitives fixed. At an entry tie the choice is set-valued; a derivative of a uniquely selected output cannot describe the jump from0 to a positive scale. This is a model implication, not empirical evidence about firms' responses.

Independent task and benchmark. Change to (4,2,4,5). The positive candidate is2, gross surplus4, net−1; zero uniquely wins. The tuple is (2,4,-1). A response “q=2 because the derivative is zero” repeats the original misconception. Ask additionally whether treating F as sunk changes the answer: if F is paid even at q=0, compare G(q)−F with−F, so output2 is preferred. The different answer follows from a different outside payoff, not an arithmetic correction to the avoidable-cost model.

Contribution, disagreement and next decision. Leon supplied the initial derivative argument; Sal supplied the operating-versus-entry distinction; Leon's revision must contain the completed-square proof and branch comparison in his own explained work. A future joint paper would need a new contribution discussion; this standard result alone is not evidence of novelty. Suppose Sal says “remove the zero-output branch to make the result elegant.” Leon's proposed response is: “With an avoidable F=10, output3 yields−1 while zero yields0. Removing nonentry changes the model's optimum. I can present a conditional operating-scale proposition, explicitly conditional on operation, alongside the entry result. Please choose between that scoped statement and a clearly labeled sunk-cost model.” Preserve the mathematical counterexample and decision. If pressure to misstate the result persists, pause external circulation and consult an appropriate independent research or program contact through the actual process; do not resolve the disagreement by concealing the counterexample.

5. Assess independence and revise the relationship

For these cases, use four two-point criteria: target/domain clarity; correct calculation or global argument; interpretation and limits; transparent assistance and a reasoned changed-task response. Award two for complete evidence, one for partial evidence with a localized gap, zero for absent or contrary evidence. This eight-point local rubric organizes feedback; it is not a validated independence scale. A causal overclaim in Case A or failure to compare with nonentry in Case B requires repair even if presentation earns other points. Assess the exact work, not confidence, speed or deference.

At a milestone review, decide whether to continue, narrow, extend or stop. Record what was accomplished, what failed, why, and what evidence would change the decision. A negative result can complete a well-defined question. If access fails, a theoretical sensitivity analysis can replace an empirical claim only after the target and deliverable are changed openly. Mentoring also includes helping the learner seek a second methodological perspective when the supervisor lacks expertise; referrals should not be disguised as a guarantee of placement, publication or approval.

Exercises

  1. Replace “Prove the program worked; send something soon” with a complete short scope agreement for Case A. Include the target, exclusions, roles, feasible workload, product, review criterion and a response to unavailable real data.
  2. Using Case A's original table, derive the alternative decomposition with final shares weighting wage changes. Give both components, their sum and the interaction; write a three-sentence feedback message explaining why a different allocation does not disprove the first identity.
  3. A student reports that the changed-data task proves every worker gained because the aggregate rose. Write a complete corrected paragraph using the changed-data results and a follow-up question with its full answer. Explain why fixed shares do not establish a within-person change.
  4. For the avoidable-cost model use(a,b,K,F)=(8,2,3,14), then F=15, then F=16. Input: (8,2,3,14). Solve all global choices with payoffs, identify the capacity condition and write targeted feedback to “a/b=4, so output4.”
  5. A supervisor claims “Strict concavity guarantees a unique global quantity for every F≥0.” Supply a numerical counterexample in the stated model and a full short corrected proposition. Handle a=0 and explain why a tie does not imply every intermediate q is optimal.
  6. Write a contribution and credit memo after Mira designs the question and analysis, a research assistant performs documented data checks, and Arun contributes a new identification strategy for a possible extension. Distinguish the completed descriptive exercise from the proposed joint paper, and specify a review process without assigning universal authorship rights.
  7. A supervisor cancels two meetings, demands unrelated work and says a complaint must be discussed only with them. Write a usable student message and an alternative escalation plan. Include interim project scope, records, an independent contact and limits of confidentiality; do not invent an institutional policy or presume misconduct has been established.
  8. Write a three-stage plan for assessing Leon's growing independence after the corrected proof. Supply an actual new task and full answer, record permitted help, and explain what evidence would justify progression or remediation. Use(a,b,K,F)=(2,1,1,3/2) for the new task: (2,1,1,3/2).
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

1. A feasible descriptive agreement

“Mira will decompose the change in mean nominal hourly wages in the supplied synthetic two-group table into within-group and share-change terms, using initial shares for the first term. The deliverable in four weeks is a two-page descriptive memo, exact table and reproducible calculation. We exclude program effects, real purchasing power and individual trajectories. Mira owns the calculation and draft; Arun reviews the target, one decomposition and one revision, returning comments within two working days of scheduled review. Six student hours weekly include a30-minute meeting. Week1 requires correct units and means, week2 a reconciled identity, week3 claims matched to evidence, week4 a changed-data defense. We will disclose substantive assistance. If proposed real data are unavailable, the synthetic descriptive exercise remains the agreed task; we will not invent observations or imply access. Any empirical extension needs a revised target, access review and schedule.” Evaluate the presence and coherence of all requested elements, rather than wording. A date alone or ‘work harder’ is not a milestone criterion.

2. Reference weights and an interaction

Add and subtractΣsg1wg0: Δμ=Σsg1Δwg+ΣΔsgwg0. The components are(1/5)2+(4/5)4=18/5 and(−3/5)20+(3/5)40=12; the sum is78/5. The interaction is(−3/5)2+(3/5)4=6/5. It is added to the original wage term12/5 and subtracted from the original share term66/5. Feedback: “Your alternative components correctly sum to the same observed15.6. The1.2 interaction is assigned to a different component because you changed the reference weights. State that convention and retain the descriptive interpretation; neither identity identifies a causal program effect.” Full credit requires the identity, all four numbers, the allocation explanation and actionable feedback.

3. The aggregate does not describe every person

“The changed table has final mean34.6, giving aggregate growth53/120≈44.17%. At initial shares the final mean is24.4, growth1/60≈1.67%; the within-group and composition terms are0.4 and10.2 currency units per hour. Group H's mean falls from40 to38, so even group averages do not all rise. No individual trajectories are supplied, and neither calculation identifies the program's effect.” Follow-up: “If final shares instead equal the initial shares but final wages remain21 and38, what is the aggregate change?” Answer: final mean24.4, change0.4 and growth1/60; composition is zero. Even then a group mean can change because its membership changes, so fixed group weights do not establish what happened to the same people. Credit numerical accuracy, the counterexample to ‘every’, the solved follow-up and the individual-versus-group distinction.

4. Capacity and nonentry

The unconstrained positive scale is8/2=4>3, so q*=3. Gross surplus is8·3−(2/2)3²=15. At F=14, operating net1 beats zero; at15,0 and3 tie at0; at16, operating net−1 loses to zero. The candidate/net sequence is (3,15,1,3,15,0,3,15,-1). Feedback: “Your derivative identifies the unconstrained gross maximum, but4 violates K=3. Evaluate the feasible boundary3 and compare its net payoff with the outside option separately for each fixed cost. The same operating candidate can support entry, a tie or nonentry.” A complete answer names all global choices; reporting the best operating scale alone is incomplete.

5. A precise uniqueness claim

With(a,b,K,F)=(6,2,4,9), both0 and3 yield0; hence the claimed uniqueness fails. For a>0, q*=min{K,a/b} uniquely maximizes gross operating surplus S. Compare S−F with0: choose q* uniquely if positive,0 uniquely if negative, and exactly{0,q*} if zero. For a=0, every positive payoff is strictly negative, so0 uniquely wins even if F=0. The quadratic has only one positive gross maximizer; every other positive q has a strictly smaller value. In the counterexample q=3/2 yields9−9/4−9=−9/4, so it is not optimal despite lying between0 and3. The discontinuity in the avoidable-cost payoff at0 prevents applying a global strict-concavity claim to that whole payoff function.

6. A provisional contribution memo

“The completed descriptive exercise records Mira's question, calculation and drafting; the assistant's named data checks with dates and outputs; and Arun's feedback. A possible extension now adds Arun's identification strategy. We will preserve the exercise's provenance and open a separate ledger for the proposed paper: question/design, data construction, code, analysis, interpretation and drafting, each linked to actual work and review responsibility. We will discuss prospective author and acknowledgement roles with all contributors, inspect the relevant venue and institutional criteria, and revisit the agreement at design freeze and before submission. We will not promise automatic author status for supervision or access, or exclude the assistant solely by job title. We will agree who checks which claims and ensure each proposed author can meet applicable responsibilities. Unresolved credit will go through an appropriate independent process before submission; data access and ownership questions require their own applicable agreements.” Evaluate accurate attribution, the changed project boundary, inclusion of contributors and a concrete revisiting process. The supplied contributions do not by themselves determine a universally correct author list or order.

7. A documented route that does not depend on permission to seek advice

Message: “Our agreed milestones depend on feedback on the decomposition. The last two meetings did not occur. I propose a written review by the end of next week and a replacement meeting, or an agreed alternative reviewer. Until we revise scope, I will continue the six-hour descriptive project; please specify the new task's project, expected time and credit separately. I will keep the current draft and decision log available through our authorized workspace. I may seek independent advice about the agreement and available routes.” Alternative plan: retain dated cancellations, requests and relevant versions; verify a program director, graduate adviser, ombuds or other appropriate independent contact and their role before sharing sensitive details. Ask about confidentiality and reporting limits rather than assuming a private conversation stays confidential. Seek an interim review/access arrangement and clarification of duties; do not distribute restricted data. If approaching the supervisor is unsafe or the concern is more serious than scheduling, use the actual available institutional support/reporting route directly. This records a dispute and asks for help; it neither proves misconduct nor promises a remedy. Credit a concrete message, interim scope, records, independent route and honest limits.

8. A progression based on work

Stage1: with the corrected proof available, Leon explains why a derivative omits avoidable entry cost and identifies every assumption; Sal records any prompts. Stage2: Leon works individually on(a,b,K,F)=(2,1,1,3/2), with the model statement and calculator permitted but no solution or substantive collaboration. Since a/b=2>K=1, the best positive scale is1, gross surplus2−1/2=3/2 and net0. Exactly0 and1 tie; q=1/2 gives1−1/8−3/2=−5/8. The benchmark is (1,3/2,0,-5/8). Stage3: Leon chooses and defends a next question: “What changes if the cost is sunk?” He must change the outside payoff to−3/2 and show that q=1 uniquely beats it, while explaining that this is a different economic assumption. Preserve all work and assistance. Progress to a new model only after the domain, global comparison and changed-assumption reasoning are demonstrated on the actual artifacts; remediate a missing outside option with another contrast and reassess later. This plan supplies criteria and a benchmark, not evidence that Leon has passed or become an independent researcher.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain in three minutes why correcting a student and assessing the student's independence are separate acts. Use one exact error from each case and propose the next artifact. Answer guide: Case A needs a descriptive decomposition and removal of a causal claim, followed by an independently interpreted changed table. Case B needs a capacity/global-entry comparison, followed by a new parameter or sunk-cost task. Attribute supplied reasoning, retain the revision and evaluate the changed task under explicit help conditions. Do not equate politeness, speed or agreement with understanding.

Delayed check. After a gap, without the solutions, use unchanged wages20 and40, initial L share4/5 and final L share1/2. Compute the means and initial-weight decomposition; state what remains unidentified. Then set a=0,b=2,K=4,F=0 in the firm model and defend the global choice. Full answer: the means are24 and30, growth1/4; wage-change contribution0, composition6. Those exact results are (24,30,1/4,0,6). Group wages do not change but the aggregate does; no individual or program effect follows. Every positive firm output has payoff−q²<0, so zero uniquely wins. An actual later response would be retention evidence for these arguments; this printed answer is not.

Sources, boundaries and next work

The three linked professional sources were inspected in their bounded official HTML bodies: ORI's Chapter7 introduction and basic responsibilities, and the AEA's2018 code. They support the stated professional principles; the agreements, cases, feedback, decompositions, proof, exercises and scoring are original. No linked institutional rule, empirical mentoring-effect study or universal authorship criterion is claimed. For an actual project, inspect the relevant institution's supervision, data, credit and dispute procedures and the proposed publication's criteria; obtain appropriate advice on questions outside the supervisor's competence. The next chapter, Communication to policymakers and boards, extends careful claims and explicit responsibilities to decision-facing communication.

Sources and further study

  • ORI Introduction to RCR, Chapter 7 — Mentor and Trainee Responsibilities: Introduction — Bounded professional guidance on mutual responsibilities, supportive research conditions, supervision and development toward independent research; potential time/credit conflicts.
  • ORI Introduction to RCR, Chapter 7 — Basic responsibilities — Early expectations, criteria, shared duties, data practices and credit; unequal power and mentor responsibility to raise sensitive issues.
  • American Economic Association — Code of Professional Conduct — Honesty/care/transparency, limits of expertise, conflicts, respectful economic discussion and fair treatment.
